claims.text: `git bisect start` opens a bisect session; `git bisect bad` with no argument marks the commit currently checked out as failing, and `git bisect good <commit>` marks a named commit as passing.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, 'Basic bisect commands: start, bad, good'

claims.text: Once one bad and one good commit are known, Git checks out a commit between them and waits for the next good/bad answer; each answer discards the half of the range the answer rules out, and the session ends when one candidate is left.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, DESCRIPTION (binary search, 'Bisecting: N revisions left to test')

claims.text: Marking a commit bad tells Git the first bad commit is that commit or an earlier one; marking it good tells it the first bad commit is a later one. The search only works if the check passes up to one commit and fails from then on — an assumption you supply, not one Git can check.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, DESCRIPTION and 'Bisect terms'

claims.text: When one candidate remains, Git prints `<full id> is the first bad commit` followed by that commit's details, including its message and the files it changed.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, DESCRIPTION (final output of a bisect session)

claims.text: `git bisect reset` ends the session and returns to the branch that was checked out before the session started.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, 'Bisect reset'

claims.text: The number of steps is about log₂ of the number of commits between the two ends: four commits take two steps, a thousand about ten.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, DESCRIPTION ('roughly N steps' in the progress line); binary search on a range of N

claims.text: A check that can answer differently at the same commit can flip one answer; the search then throws away the half that holds the real cause and ends on some other commit. Nothing in Git catches this, so the answer is only as trustworthy as the check.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, DESCRIPTION and 'git bisect skip' (commits that cannot be tested); outline item 2 of foundation.l2.git-bisect

claims.text: `HEAD` is the commit currently checked out; `HEAD~4` names the commit four steps back from it along first parents; `git switch --detach <commit>` checks that commit out without being on a branch, and `git switch -` returns to the branch checked out before.
claims.source_hint: gitrevisions documentation, `<rev>~<n>`; git-switch documentation, --detach and `-`

claims.text: Opinion: when the two ends are far apart and you have no suspicion about where the change is, bisect costs less than reading the diffs, because the work grows with log₂ of the range rather than with the range.
claims.source_hint: outline items 1 and 2 of foundation.l2.git-bisect

claims.text: Opinion: when commits are small and single-purpose, the commit a bisect names usually explains the failure by itself; when one commit holds a week of work, the same search still finishes but names a change too large to read.
claims.source_hint: outline items 3 and 4 of foundation.l2.git-bisect

claims.text: Opinion: choose a good commit older than you suspect rather than one close to the failure, because a good end that is in fact already bad makes the answer wrong while a distant one only adds a step or two.
claims.source_hint: outline item 1 of foundation.l2.git-bisect; git-bisect documentation, DESCRIPTION (the good end must precede the first bad commit)

claims.text: A range of a few dozen commits (24 to 64) is settled in five or six runs of the check, since ceil(log₂ 24) = 5 and ceil(log₂ 64) = 6.
claims.source_hint: git-bisect documentation, DESCRIPTION (the 'Bisecting: N revisions left to test after this (roughly M steps)' progress lines, where M is log₂ of N)
